nameStory: The name 'cocklebur' comes from the spiny, burr-like fruits that cling tenaciously to clothing, fur, and feathers - much like the spiny shells of cockles (marine mollusks). These hitchhiking seed pods are so effective at grabbing onto anything that passes by that they've become the poster child for annoying plants that follow you home from nature walks.
description: Common cocklebur is a sturdy annual weed that grows 1-4 feet tall with broad, rough leaves and an upright, branching habit. This member of the sunflower family produces small, inconspicuous greenish flowers followed by its signature feature: oval, spiny burs about an inch long. The entire plant has a coarse, somewhat weedy appearance and feels rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Oval burs about 1 inch long, covered in hooked spines that grab onto clothing and fur with remarkable tenacity - they're genuinely difficult to pull off once attached

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, triangular to heart-shaped leaves with toothed edges that feel rough and sandpapery to the touch, arranged alternately on the stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish, inconspicuous flower heads clustered along the upper stems - easy to miss as they lack the showy petals typical of other sunflower family members

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, branching annual that grows 1-4 feet tall with a somewhat sprawling, weedy appearance and thick, sturdy stems

habitat: Common cocklebur thrives in disturbed soils, waste areas, roadsides, and field edges throughout New England. It particularly favors rich, moist soils and can often be found along riverbanks, in agricultural areas, and anywhere the ground has been recently disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Young seedlings emerge with their characteristic rough, triangular leaves beginning to develop.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce small greenish flowers from July through August, with the rough leaves becoming more prominent.
seasonality.fall: The notorious spiny burs ripen and become ready to hitchhike on passing animals and humans - peak 'sticking season' runs from September through October.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried burs still attached, continuing to disperse seeds throughout the cold months.

funFact: Cocklebur burs were the inspiration for Velcro! In 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral examined cocklebur burs stuck to his dog's fur under a microscope and discovered the tiny hooks that grab onto loops in fabric and fur, leading him to invent the hook-and-loop fastener we know today.
confusionNotes: The spiny burs make cocklebur nearly impossible to confuse with other plants once they're present. Before the burs develop, the rough, triangular leaves might be confused with some members of the goosefoot family, but cocklebur's leaves feel much more sandpapery and the plant structure is sturdier.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' cocklebur, this species was actually introduced to North America and has become naturalized. The burs can be toxic to livestock if eaten in large quantities, containing compounds that can cause liver damage in cattle and pigs.
compareHints: Common cocklebur is very similar to rough cocklebur, but tends to have slightly smaller burs with more densely packed spines. Beach cocklebur, found in coastal areas, typically has more deeply lobed leaves and grows in sandier soils. All three species share the characteristic hitchhiking burs that make cockleburs instantly recognizable as a group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rough cocklebur is distinguished from common cocklebur by its larger burrs and more deeply lobed leaves with a distinctly rougher texture.
Beach cocklebur differs from rough cocklebur and common cocklebur primarily in its coastal habitat and thicker, more succulent leaves that help it survive salt spray and sandy conditions.
